title: Moses Murdered a Man and Ran Away — God Still Wasn’t Finished With His Story
paragraphs: Moses Murdered a Man and Ran Away — God Still Wasn’t Finished With His Story

He buried a man in the sand, fled the life he knew, and disappeared into the wilderness. Then, decades later, God called his name from a fire that refused to go out. If you think your worst chapter has already written the ending of your life, Moses has something to tell you.
There was a body beneath the sand.
And Moses knew exactly how it got there.
Before the Red Sea.
Before the plagues.
Before Pharaoh heard the words, “Let my people go.”
Before Sinai trembled.
Before the tablets of stone.
Before generations would speak his name as one of the defining figures of Scripture...
there was an Egyptian lying dead.
And Moses had killed him.
That detail matters because sometimes we remember biblical heroes after grace has finished telling their story.
We remember Moses with the staff in his hand.
God remembers the entire man.
The frightened baby hidden among the reeds.
The adopted son raised in Pharaoh’s household.
The Hebrew who saw the suffering of his people.
The man who became violent.
The fugitive who ran.
The shepherd who disappeared into obscurity.
The trembling man standing barefoot before a burning bush.
The reluctant servant.
The leader.
The intercessor.
The sinner who needed grace.
And if you have ever looked backward at something you did and wondered whether God could possibly do anything meaningful with the person who did it...
do not leave this story too quickly.
Because there is something buried in the sand.
And eventually, Moses discovered that sand cannot bury what God already knows.
Exodus 2 tells the story with uncomfortable simplicity. Moses went out to his Hebrew brothers and witnessed their forced labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Then Scripture says:
“וַיַּךְ אֶת־הַמִּצְרִי וַיִּטְמְנֵהוּ בַּחוֹל”
Vayyakh et-hammitzri vayitmenehu bachol.
In straightforward English:
“He struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.”
That is the force of Exodus 2:12.

The Hebrew does not allow us to turn this into a harmless misunderstanding. The verb נכה (nakah), appearing here in the form וַיַּךְ (vayyakh), carries the idea of striking or striking down. What follows makes the outcome unmistakable: Moses hides the Egyptian in the sand, and the next day another Hebrew confronts him about killing the Egyptian.

Acts 7 later retells the event explicitly: Moses saw an Israelite being mistreated, defended him, and struck down the Egyptian. Stephen also tells us something important about Moses' thinking: Moses apparently believed his own people would understand that God was giving them deliverance through him.
They did not understand.
That makes the tragedy deeper.
Moses seems to have sensed something real about his connection to Israel and perhaps even about his role in their deliverance.
But sensing a calling is not the same thing as being ready to fulfill it.
He saw oppression.
He cared.
He acted.
But he acted disastrously.
And there is a warning here for every passionate believer.
You can care about something God cares about and still respond to it in a way God has not commanded.
A right burden does not automatically sanctify a wrong method.
Moses could not manufacture God's deliverance through human violence.
God would indeed use Moses to confront Egypt—but God's deliverance would unfold according to God's command, God's timing, and God's power.
There is a difference between being used by God and trying to play God.
Moses had not learned that difference yet.
Look at the scene.
Before striking the Egyptian, Moses looked around.
He looked this way.
Then that way.
No one.
Or so he thought.
There is something painfully human about that moment.
Have you ever done something you would never have done if the right person had been watching?
Have you ever checked the room?
Deleted the message?
Cleared the history?
Closed the tab?
Changed the story?
Hidden the receipt?
Covered the tracks?
Practiced the explanation?
Smiled in church while carrying something inside you that you desperately hoped nobody would discover?
Moses looked around.
But he did not look up.
And by the next day, his secret was already talking.
Two Hebrews were fighting. Moses confronted the one in the wrong.
The man's answer must have hit like a knife:
“Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?”
Then Scripture gives us four terrifying words:
“Moses was afraid.”
The secret was out.
Pharaoh heard about it.
Pharaoh wanted Moses dead.
And Moses ran. Exodus records his flight to Midian, while Acts likewise recounts that after the killing became known, Moses fled and lived as a foreigner there.
Imagine that journey.
Behind him was Egypt.
Behind him was privilege.
Behind him was the palace.
Behind him was a dead man.
Behind him was a warrant for his life.
Ahead of him?
Desert.
Silence.
Uncertainty.
Moses went from Pharaoh's household to the wilderness.
From somebody to nobody.
From proximity to power to tending another man's sheep.
And perhaps you understand that kind of wilderness better than you wish you did.
Maybe nobody is chasing you across a desert.
But you know what it is to run mentally from yesterday.
You know what it is to replay a decision at 2:17 in the morning.
You know what it is to wonder what your life would look like if you had chosen differently.
If you had not slept with that person.
If you had not betrayed that trust.
If you had controlled your anger.
If you had not walked away.
If you had told the truth.
If you had stayed sober.
If you had listened.
If you had not wasted those years.
If you had not wounded the people you loved.
Some consequences cannot simply be undone.
Christianity does not require us to pretend otherwise.
Grace is not calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not God developing amnesia.
Redemption does not mean sin was secretly harmless.
A man was dead.
Moses had fled.
Nothing about God's later use of Moses makes that death insignificant.
And that is precisely why this story is so powerful.
The Bible does not need to airbrush its servants to prove the power of God.
It tells us the scandal...
because the glory belongs to God.
Then something astonishing happens.
Years pass.
Not hours.
Not a weekend.
Not one emotional worship service followed by an instant comeback.
Years.
Acts 7 places Moses' life in striking stages and says that forty years passed before the burning-bush encounter.
Forty years.
Think about that.
Long enough for Egypt to become a memory.
Long enough for the fugitive to become a husband and father.
Long enough for royal rhythms to be replaced by sheep.
Long enough, perhaps, for Moses to assume that whatever his life might once have become was over.
And then...
fire.
A bush was burning.
But it was not consumed.
Moses turned aside.
And from the place where he expected nothing extraordinary, God spoke his name:
“Moses, Moses.”
What must it have felt like to discover that heaven still knew your name?
Moses had changed addresses.
God had not lost him.
Moses had disappeared into Midian.
God had not misplaced him.
Moses had a history.
God already knew it.
Moses had become a shepherd.
God was preparing to send him to shepherd a nation.
The wilderness that looked like the burial ground of Moses' calling became the landscape where God summoned him.
But notice what Scripture does not teach.
God did not say, “Moses, murder doesn't matter.”
God did not celebrate Moses' sin.
God did not tell him his choices were irrelevant because everything eventually worked out.
Biblical grace never requires God to lower His holiness.
Instead, the story reveals something far greater:
Human sin does not make God less sovereign.
Moses' failure was real.
God's purpose was greater.
And when God called Moses, He did not call him because murder had somehow become acceptable.
He called him according to His covenant purposes and mercy.
Stephen later describes the stunning reversal: the Moses who had been rejected with the question, “Who made you ruler and judge?” became the very Moses God sent as ruler and deliverer.
Do you see it?
The accusation from Moses' past did not become the final sentence over Moses' future.
And maybe that is where this story has finally reached you.
Because somewhere inside you there may be a sentence you have been repeating for years.
“God could never use someone like me.”
“I knew better.”
“I went too far.”
“I ruined everything.”
“People would look at me differently if they knew.”
“I wasted my opportunity.”
“My family will never forgive me.”
“I cannot become the person I should have been.”
Maybe you have spent years hiding your own Egypt beneath emotional sand.
Listen carefully.
Moses' story does not give you permission to minimize your sin.
It gives you permission to stop believing that your sin is more powerful than God's ability to redeem a repentant sinner.
Those are very different things.
And this is where Moses' story must lead us beyond Moses.
Because Moses is not the Savior of this article.
Jesus is.
Moses was a deliverer, but he himself was a sinful man in need of God.
Jesus Christ is the greater Deliverer.
Moses fled after the death of another man.
Jesus willingly walked toward His own death.
Moses could lead Israel out of physical slavery, but he could not cleanse the human heart from sin.
Jesus came to deal with the slavery beneath every other slavery.
Sin.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Death.
At the cross, God did not sweep sin beneath cosmic sand.
He dealt with it.
This is why grace can never mean, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross declares the opposite.
Sin matters so terribly that reconciliation with a holy God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Christ bore sin and judgment, and He rose again.
That is why the Gospel is infinitely better than self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to help guilty people become slightly nicer guilty people.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Reconcile.
Redeem.
Make new.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Your salvation is not purchased by becoming impressive enough to erase yesterday.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
The Christian hope is that Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
So repentance is not pretending the body beneath the sand never existed.
Repentance brings the truth into the light.
It stops defending.
Stops hiding.
Stops renaming sin.
Stops blaming everybody else.
And turns toward God.
Grace meets us there—not as permission to continue living in rebellion, but as God's undeserved favor that leads us into a transformed life.
Maybe your Egypt is calling you right now.
Maybe there is something you need to confess to God.
Maybe there is someone you need to ask forgiveness from.
Maybe restitution is possible and appropriate.
Maybe accountability needs to begin.
Maybe the secret has been eating you alive because you have spent more energy hiding than healing.
Do not confuse hiding with repentance.
Moses buried something in sand.
God eventually brought Moses onto holy ground.
Sand is where humans hide things.
Holy ground is where we stop pretending before God.
And perhaps that is why the burning bush feels so breathtaking.
The same Moses who once looked around to make sure nobody saw him eventually stood before the God who sees everything.
And God still spoke his name.
Not because Moses deserved a second chapter.
Grace, by definition, is not wages.
God spoke.
“Moses.”
The fugitive heard his name.
“Moses.”
The shepherd heard his name.
“Moses.”
The failed would-be deliverer heard his name.
And the man who once ran from Egypt would eventually be commanded to walk back toward it.
God did not merely give Moses something to do.
He dismantled Moses' confidence in himself.
When Moses first acted in Egypt, he seemed ready to take matters into his own hands.
At the burning bush, he sounded profoundly different.
“Who am I?”
That question matters.
The man who once behaved as though strength were enough had learned weakness.
And God's answer was not a motivational speech about Moses discovering how extraordinary Moses really was.
God's answer was better:
“I will be with you.”
That is the center.
Not Moses.
God.
Not your greatness.
Christ.
Not the heroic reconstruction of your personal brand.
Grace.
The Gospel does not tell broken sinners to stare into mirrors until they become convinced they are powerful.
It tells sinners to look to Jesus Christ.
Your hope is not that you can rewrite everything.
Jesus Christ is the One who saves, redeems, restores, and transforms.
And no, that does not mean every consequence disappears.

Moses' story is not a promise that every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was, every earthly opportunity returned, every legal consequence removed, or every dream revived in precisely the form you wanted.
Biblical redemption is bigger than getting your old life back.
Sometimes God does not return you to the life you lost.
He makes you faithful in a life you never imagined.
Moses probably could not have imagined, while walking into Midian as a fugitive, that decades later he would stand before Pharaoh.
He could not see the sea opening.
He could not hear Israel singing on the opposite shore.
He could not see Sinai.
He could not know that centuries later Stephen would still be telling his story.
He could not see that readers thousands of years later would find themselves somewhere between the sand and the burning bush.
But God could see farther than Moses' failure.
And He can see farther than yours.
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing the truth into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Someone else reading may need to discover that they are not the only believer trying to trust God in the wilderness.
The church was never meant to be a museum where everybody displays polished versions of themselves.
We are people desperately dependent upon the mercy of Jesus.
Send this article to the person who thinks their worst chapter disqualified them forever.
Someone may need the Gospel tonight.
Someone may have concluded that Jesus wants nothing to do with people who have failed badly.
Someone needs to hear that repentance is still possible, mercy is still real, and Christ still saves sinners.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Not to glorify Moses.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify your own comeback.
Glorify Christ.
Because the greatest message in Moses' story is not that a murderer became famous.
It is that God remained God when Moses' life fell apart.
The God who met Moses in the wilderness is holy.
The God who judges sin is holy.
The God who keeps His covenant is holy.
And the Gospel reveals how holy God can justify sinners without ceasing to be righteous: through Jesus Christ.
So bring Him the thing you buried.
Bring Him the years you regret.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the version of yourself you wish nobody had ever seen.
Do not bring it as an excuse.
Bring it in repentance.
And look to Christ.
You may have made decisions that changed your life permanently.
You may carry scars until you die.
You may have consequences grace does not magically erase.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your sin does not get to occupy the throne.
Jesus does.
The cross has spoken.
The tomb is empty.
Grace is not pretending your scandal never happened.
Grace is discovering that your scandal does not have authority to write the final sentence when your life has been surrendered to Christ.
Moses buried a man in the sand.
God met Moses in the wilderness.
And generations later, Scripture still tells both parts of the story.
Maybe that is what you needed tonight.
God does not need an edited version of your history before you come to Him.
He already knows.
Come anyway.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop running.
There is mercy in Jesus Christ for sinners who come to Him.
And when your past whispers, “Look what you did,” remember where the Gospel teaches the repentant sinner to look:
Look what Christ has done.
Save that sentence.
Because somewhere, somebody is still running through Midian convinced that failure was the last page.
Let them see that Jesus Christ still saves.
Let them see that grace does not erase the truth.
Grace changes who gets the final word.
You may still remember the sand—but in Christ, the sand does not get to write your ending.
